summary: Defines a common set of data types and parsing rules, called Structured Fields, so that new HTTP header and trailer fields can use one strict, well-defined syntax instead of each inventing its own. This makes such fields easier and safer to define and handle. It was replaced by RFC 9651.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of every HTTP header being written in its own odd style, this gives them all a shared set of building blocks, like standard Lego bricks.

questions: how to define a new http header field syntax
why use structured fields instead of json
what data types do structured fields support
how do you serialize a structured field
subtitle: A standard syntax for HTTP header and trailer field values.

tldr.problem: Each new HTTP header field invents its own syntax, making them inconsistent, difficult to parse correctly, and prone to security issues. Different implementations handle similar-looking header values in incompatible ways.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8941 defines a small set of standardized data types (Lists, Dictionaries, and Items) with strict parsing and serialization algorithms. Any new HTTP header or trailer that uses these types gets the same predictable syntax.
tldr.outcome: HTTP specifications that use Structured Fields are simpler to write and implement, safer from parsing errors, and easier to extend without breaking existing parsers. The specification was later refined and replaced by RFC 9651.

today: RFC 8941 is a Proposed Standard. It has been superseded by RFC 9651, which refines and clarifies the specification based on implementation experience.

sections.title: The HTTP Header Problem
sections.content:
Defining the syntax of a new HTTP header field is surprisingly difficult. Without a standard to follow, each header invents its own format—some use commas, some use semicolons, some use quotes or special characters in incompatible ways. This forces every HTTP library to write custom parsing code for each header, introducing bugs and interoperability problems. Even worse, when intermediaries or different software components modify a header, a small parsing mistake in one can corrupt the entire field for everyone downstream.

RFC 8941 solves this by providing a common syntax for HTTP header and trailer fields. New specifications can reference this standard instead of inventing their own format, gaining reliability and consistency for free.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine every restaurant wrote their menu in a different language and format. Structured Fields gives all restaurants the same format, so customers only need to learn one system.

sections.title: Three Core Data Types
sections.content:
Structured Fields defines three top-level types that an HTTP field value can be. A List is a comma-separated sequence of members, each of which can be a single item or a grouped set of items in parentheses (an inner list). A Dictionary is a set of key-value pairs, where keys are short text strings and values can be items or inner lists. An Item is a single value, optionally followed by parameters (key-value pairs introduced with a semicolon).

For example, a header defined as a List of tokens might look like sugar, tea, rum. A Dictionary might look like en="hello", da=:binary: with byte sequences. Every member can carry optional parameters for extensibility, allowing future versions of a field to add new information without breaking existing parsers.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of containers: a List (items in a row, separated by commas), a Dictionary (named values, like a phone book), and single Items. Every field uses one of these three shapes.

sections.title: Item Types and Values
sections.content:
Within Lists, Dictionaries, and Inner Lists, the actual values are Items, each of which has a type. An Integer ranges from -999,999,999,999,999 to 999,999,999,999,999 (15 digits signed, for IEEE 754 compatibility). A Decimal has an integer part (up to 12 digits) and a fractional part (up to 3 digits), written as 4.5. A String is text in double quotes, like "hello world", with backslash escaping for quotes and backslashes themselves.

A Token is a short unquoted word like foo123, used for enumerated values or identifiers. A Byte Sequence is binary data encoded in base64 between colons: :cHJldGVuZA==:. Finally, a Boolean is either true (?1) or false (?0). This set of types covers the vast majority of data that HTTP headers need to carry.
sections.plainLanguage: Items come in six flavors: numbers (integers or decimals), text in quotes (strings), words without quotes (tokens), true/false (booleans), and encoded binary (byte sequences).

sections.title: Serializing and Parsing
sections.content:
The RFC defines precise step-by-step algorithms for converting between the abstract data types and their wire representation in HTTP fields. When serializing (turning data into bytes), an empty List or Dictionary is omitted entirely; parameters whose value is the Boolean true omit the =true part. When parsing (reading bytes and extracting data), each algorithm is deliberately strict: if the input does not match the expected format exactly, parsing fails for the entire field value. This strict approach is intentional—it forces producers to generate correct output and catches mistakes early, rather than letting them propagate silently.

Implementations must handle fields that span multiple header lines (the HTTP specification allows that), but individual values cannot be split across lines. If parsing fails for any reason, the entire field is ignored, preventing ambiguity or corruption from spreading downstream.
sections.plainLanguage: There are strict rules for how to write Structured Fields down on the wire and how to read them back. If something looks wrong, reject the whole field instead of guessing. This stops one broken header from confusing everything downstream.

sections.title: Security and Limits
sections.content:
Because most types in Structured Fields have no hard size limit, extremely large field values could be used to exhaust memory or CPU resources. HTTP implementations typically limit the total size of headers or individual fields to defend against this. The specification defines minimum sizes that all parsers must support (at least 1024 members in a List, 256 members in an Inner List, 256 parameters on an Item, 1024 characters in a String, 512 characters in a Token, and 16384 octets in a Byte Sequence after decoding), but not maximums.

The other main security concern is field injection: if an attacker can add new HTTP fields to a message, they might be able to change the meaning of a Structured Field. Implementations should validate that fields they process come from a trusted source. The strict parsing rules help: if an injected field cannot be parsed, it will be safely ignored rather than misinterpreted.
sections.plainLanguage: Huge field values could cause denial-of-service attacks, so implementations set limits. And if someone injects a fake header, strict parsing rejects it rather than accidentally using it.
